--- title: "Graph Theory: Equivalence & Similarity" subtitle: "The Positional Structure of Social Networks" format: revealjs: scrollable: true theme: default css: ucla-theme.css width: 1280 height: 720 margin: 0.1 min-scale: 0.2 --- # Part 1: The Positional Approach & Structural Equivalence --- ## The Position Approach ::: {.incremental} - In social network analysis, we can partition nodes using two different philosophies: 1. **The Group Approach**: Nodes are divided into subsets that are tightly interconnected with one another. 2. **The Positional Approach**: Nodes are divided into subsets based on how **similar** they are in their patterns of connectivity with others. - Nodes in the same positional class are said to occupy the same **position** or **role** in the social structure. - We distinguish between: - **Structural Equivalence**: Nodes are connected to the exact same other nodes. - **Regular Equivalence**: Nodes are connected to equivalent others (e.g., all teachers are connected to students, even if they are different students). ::: --- ## Defining Structural Equivalence :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Structural Equivalence** (Lorrain & White, 1971): - Two nodes are structurally equivalent if they are connected to the **same other nodes**. - Their patterns of connectivity are mathematically identical. - In the graph on the right: - $\{C, D\}$ are structurally equivalent because both are connected to $\{A, B, E\}$. - $\{A, B\}$ are structurally equivalent because both are connected to $\{C, D\}$. - $\{E\}$ and $\{F\}$ occupy **unique positions** (neighborhoods are not shared). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](positional-equivalence_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Adjacency Matrix of Equivalent Positions ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
A B C D E F
A 0 0 1 1 0 0
B 0 0 1 1 0 0
C 1 1 0 0 1 0
D 1 1 0 0 1 0
E 0 0 1 1 0 1
F 0 0 0 0 1 0
````` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Structurally equivalent nodes have **identical rows (and columns)** in the adjacency matrix. - Notice that Row A is identical to Row B ($0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0$), and Row C is identical to Row D ($1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0$). - Nodes in unique positions (like $E$ and $F$) have completely unique row patterns. ::: --- ## Structural Similarity: A Necessary Relaxation ::: {.incremental} - In real-world social networks, strict structural equivalence is **extremely rare**. - It only allows a binary "yes" or "no" answer: either nodes connect to the exact same neighbors, or they do not. - If node $A$ and node $B$ share 99 out of 100 neighbors, they are technically *not* structurally equivalent! - **Structural Similarity**: - Allows for a "more or less" gradient rather than binary classification. - Measures the extent to which two nodes have **highly overlapping** patterns of connectivity. - Let's look at how we measure this. ::: # Part 2: Measuring Structural Similarity --- ## Euclidean Distance ($d^{Euclid}_{k,l}$) ::: {.incremental} - Ronald Burt (1976) proposed measuring structural similarity by calculating the **Euclidean Distance** between the row vectors of nodes in the adjacency matrix. - For nodes $k$ and $l$, the distance is: - $$d^{Euclid}_{k,l} = \sqrt{\sum_j (a_{(k)j} - a_{(l)j})^2}$$ - **Key Properties**: - If nodes are structurally equivalent, their Euclidean distance is **exactly zero**. - The larger the distance, the **less structurally similar** the two nodes are. ::: --- ## Euclidean Distance Calculation: $A$ vs. $C$ - Let's calculate the Euclidean distance between $A$ ($0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0$) and $C$ ($1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0$): ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Vector A 0 0 1 1 0 0
Vector C 1 1 0 0 1 0
A - C (0 - 1) (0 - 1) (1 - 0) (1 - 0) (0 - 1) (0 - 0)
Difference -1 -1 1 1 -1 0
Squared Diff 1 1 1 1 1 0
````` ::: ::: - Sum of squared differences: $\sum_j (a_{(A)j} - a_{(C)j})^2 = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 5$ - Euclidean Distance: $d^{Euclid}_{A, C} = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.24$ --- ## The Structural Similarity Matrix ($S$) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
A B C D E F
A -- 0 2.24 2.24 1 1.73
B 0 -- 2.24 2.24 1 1.73
C 2.24 2.24 -- 0 2.45 1.41
D 2.24 2.24 0 -- 2.45 1.41
E 1 1 2.45 2.45 -- 2
F 1.73 1.73 1.41 1.41 2 --
````` ::: ::: - Pairs of structurally equivalent nodes ($\{A, B\}$ and $\{C, D\}$) have a distance of **0.00**. - Unique positions like $F$ have high distances to almost everyone else (e.g., $d_{A, F} = 2.45$). --- ## Euclidean Distance in Directed Graphs ::: {.incremental} - When networks contain **asymmetric (directed) ties**, we must distinguish between two behaviors: 1. **Sending Ties**: Do nodes $u$ and $v$ point to the same out-neighbors? (Row similarity) 2. **Receiving Ties**: Do nodes $u$ and $v$ receive ties from the same in-neighbors? (Column similarity) - Two directed nodes are structurally equivalent if and only if they send ties to the same others **and** receive ties from the same others. - The Euclidean distance formula expands to sum both row and column differences: - $$d^{Euclidean}_{k,l} = \sqrt{\sum_j (a_{(k)j}-a_{(l)j})^2 + \sum_i (a_{(k)i}-a_{(l)i})^2}$$ ::: --- ## Directed Similarity Example :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Consider the directed graph on the right. - Nodes with the same color are structurally equivalent under directed Euclidean distance: - $\{E, G\}$ are structurally equivalent ($d_{E, G} = 0$). They send ties to $\{C, F\}$ and receive ties from $\{D\}$. - $\{C, F\}$ are structurally equivalent ($d_{C, F} = 0$). They send ties to $\{A\}$ and receive ties from $\{A, B, E, G\}$. - Structural equivalence in directed networks elegantly maps actors into **identical social roles**. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](positional-equivalence_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: # Part 3: Measuring Similarity via Neighborhood Overlap --- ## The Intuition of Neighborhood Overlap ::: {.incremental} - Recall that the **neighborhood** of a node is the set of all other nodes adjacent to it. - **Neighborhood Overlap**: - The more neighbors two nodes have in common, the more structurally similar they are. - If you and your colleague share **100% of your friends**, you are structurally equivalent. - If you share **none of your friends**, you occupy completely different social worlds. - We can formalize this overlap using three classical set-theoretic coefficients. ::: --- ## Three Classical Coefficients ::: {.incremental} - Let $n_{ij}$ be the number of common neighbors of nodes $i$ and $j$. - Let $k_i$ and $k_j$ be the degrees of nodes $i$ and $j$. - **1. Jaccard Similarity**: - $$J_{ij} = \frac{n_{ij}}{k_i + k_j - n_{ij}}$$ - **2. Dice Similarity**: - $$D_{ij} = \frac{2n_{ij}}{k_i + k_j}$$ - **3. Cosine Similarity**: - $$C_{ij} = \frac{n_{ij}}{\sqrt{k_i k_j}}$$ - All three metrics range from **0.0** (no overlap) to **1.0** (structural equivalence). ::: --- ## Comparing Overlap Matrices ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](positional-equivalence_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: --- ## Cosine Similarity Matrix Example ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
A B C D E F G H I J
A -- 0.67 0 0 0.33 0 0 0 0.41 0.41
B -- -- 0.33 0 0.33 0 0 0 0.41 0
C -- -- -- 0.82 0.33 0 0.33 0 0.41 0
D -- -- -- -- 0.41 0 0.41 0 0 0
E -- -- -- -- -- 0 0.33 0 0 0
F -- -- -- -- -- -- 0.41 0 0 0
G -- -- -- -- -- -- -- 0 0 0
H -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- 0 0.71
I -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- 0.5
J -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- --
````` ::: ::: - Cells record Cosine Similarity between node neighborhoods. - If $C_{ij} = 0.00$, $i$ and $j$ share absolutely zero friends. - If $C_{ij} = 1.00$, $i$ and $j$ are structurally equivalent. --- ## Neighborhood Overlap in Directed Graphs ::: {.incremental} - In directed networks, neighborhood overlap splits into: - **Out-Similarity**: Overlap in outgoing ties (pointing to the same others). - **In-Similarity**: Overlap in incoming ties (receiving nominations from the same others). - **In Citation Networks** (where paper $A \rightarrow B$ means $A$ cites $B$): - **Bibliographic Coupling** (Out-Similarity): - The number of references two papers have in common. - Measures similarity in theoretical foundations or sources. - **Co-Citation** (In-Similarity): - The frequency with which two papers are cited together by subsequent papers. - Measures how much the scientific community associates their ideas. ::: --- ## Directed Cosine Equations ::: {.incremental} - Let $n_{ij}^{out}$ be the number of shared out-neighbors, and $n_{ij}^{in}$ be the shared in-neighbors. - Let $k_i^{out}$ and $k_i^{in}$ represent out-degrees and in-degrees. - **Cosine Out-Similarity**: - $$C_{ij}^{out} = \frac{n_{ij}^{out}}{\sqrt{k_i^{out} k_j^{out}}}$$ - **Cosine In-Similarity**: - $$C_{ij}^{in} = \frac{n_{ij}^{in}}{\sqrt{k_i^{in} k_j^{in}}}$$ - These directed formulas allow researchers to partition information and communication networks based on highly specific sender and receiver roles. ::: --- # Part 4: Structural, Automorphic, and Regular Equivalence --- ## Three Concepts of Equivalence ::: {.incremental} - Beyond structural equivalence (sharing the *exact same* neighbors), there are **three nested notions** of relational position: 1. **Structural Equivalence**: Identical neighborhoods ($N(u) = N(v)$). Highly strict, same-neighbor rule. 2. **Automorphic Equivalence**: Globally symmetrical/interchangeable nodes. Nodes can be swapped without changing the graph structure. 3. **Regular Equivalence**: Connection to *equivalent others*. Focuses on general roles (e.g., all doctors connect to patients). - **The Nested Hierarchy**: - $\text{Structural} \subseteq \text{Automorphic} \subseteq \text{Regular}$ - Let's explore these definitions using a symmetrical 15-node network. ::: --- ## Symmetrical 15-Node Network :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - This 15-node network has: - Two star-like components centered at hubs $B$ and $K$. - Symmetrical leaf sets $\{A,C,D,E\}$ and $\{L,M,N,O\}$. - A tightly integrated central core $\{F,G,H,I,J\}$. - $G$ connects the core to hub $B$; $J$ connects the core to hub $K$. - Let's look at how we partition this network using the three equivalence criteria. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](positional-equivalence_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## 1. Structural Equivalence :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Structural Equivalence Partition**: - Requires connection to the **exact same** neighbors. - Groups: - **Class 1**: Leaf set $\{A,C,D,E\}$ (connected only to $B$). - **Class 2**: Leaf set $\{L,M,N,O\}$ (connected only to $K$). - **All other nodes** (colored separately) are in **unique single-node classes**. - Note: Symmetrical hubs $B$ and $K$ connect to different leaves, so they are *not* structurally equivalent! ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](positional-equivalence_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## 2. Automorphic Equivalence :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Automorphic Equivalence Partition**: - Nodes that are **globally interchangeable** (symmetric swap). - groups nodes into **five classes**: - **Leaves**: $\{A,C,D,E, L,M,N,O\}$ - **Hubs**: $\{B,K\}$ (symmetric counterparts) - **Core Bridges**: $\{G,J\}$ (gates to hubs) - **Core Mid-points**: $\{H,I\}$ (internally symmetric) - **Core Top**: $\{F\}$ (symmetric only to itself) - Successfully captures the structural similarity between hubs $B$ and $K$. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](positional-equivalence_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## 3. Regular Equivalence :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Regular Equivalence Partition**: - Connects to **equivalent others** (general roles). - Groups the 15 nodes into **four roles**: - **Class 1 (Leaves)**: $\{A,C,D,E, L,M,N,O\}$ (connect *only* to Hubs) - **Class 2 (Hubs)**: $\{B,K\}$ (connect to Leaves and Core Bridges) - **Class 3 (Core Bridges)**: $\{G,J\}$ (connect to Hubs and Core nodes) - **Class 4 (Core Nodes)**: $\{F,H,I\}$ (connect to Core Bridges and Core nodes) - Elegant and highly flexible role-mapping. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](positional-equivalence_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Summary of Positional Concepts ::: {.incremental} - **Positions represent roles**: - Unlike cohesive subgroups, actors do not need to connect to each other to be in the same position; they just need to connect to others similarly. - **Structural Equivalence is the ideal limit**: - Perfect row/column matching is highly elegant but rare in real social networks. - **Structural Similarity relaxes the limit**: - Distance metrics (Euclidean) and Overlap coefficients (Jaccard, Dice, Cosine) allow us to measure degrees of positional equivalence. - **Directionality adds analytical depth**: - Directed similarity splits into In-Similarity (Co-citation) and Out-Similarity (Bibliographic coupling), providing robust tools for citation and communication analysis. :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
